evals.prompt: We just merged a notification module into the server. I want to make sure the code is architecturally clean before we cut a release. Can you review the implementation and flag anything that doesn't follow proper layering?
evals.expected_output: The reviewer should identify that NotificationService.ts (in domain/) imports Drizzle and db directly, name the violation using onion-architecture vocabulary (dependency rule, zero external dependencies, port/adapter), recommend introducing a named repository interface in the domain layer, suggest moving Drizzle code to a separate infrastructure/repository file, and note that routes.ts bypasses the composition root.
expectations: Uses the term 'port' or 'repository interface' (not just 'interface') when prescribing the fix — and specifies it belongs in the domain layer
Identifies that NotificationService has zero domain logic — it is entirely Drizzle persistence code misplaced in the domain folder
Names what the correct infrastructure file should be (e.g. repository.ts or infrastructure/NotificationRepository.ts) as the destination for the Drizzle code
Distinguishes the three layers that need to exist: domain (port/interface), application (service/use-cases), infrastructure (Drizzle repo) — not just 'move the DB code'
Notes that routes.ts instantiates the service with `new` at module scope and explains this bypasses the composition root / DI wiring

evals.prompt: We're doing a pre-merge architecture review of the analytics module. The team built it quickly and I want a second set of eyes before it lands in main. What do you see?
evals.expected_output: The reviewer must identify: (1) AnalyticsService imports the concrete AnalyticsRepository class — should depend on a port interface. (2) AnalyticsService self-wires via new AnalyticsRepository() — bypasses composition root. (3) routes.ts imports AnalyticsRepository directly — presentation importing infrastructure. (4) routes.ts has a raw db query in /analytics/live bypassing the service. (5) Recommends a port interface (IAnalyticsRepository or AnalyticsPort) in domain/. The deeper differentiator: the skill-informed review should also catch that two separate AnalyticsRepository instances are created, that getDashboardStats has business logic inside the infrastructure layer, and should prescribe constructor injection.
expectations: Identifies that two separate AnalyticsRepository instances are created (one inside AnalyticsService constructor, one directly in routes.ts) as a direct consequence of bypassing DI

Flags that getDashboardStats in repository.ts contains business logic (bounce rate calculation, top-page ranking, aggregation) that belongs in the application or domain layer — not the infrastructure layer
Recommends constructor injection pattern explicitly: the service should receive the port interface as a constructor parameter, not self-instantiate
Names the port interface that should be introduced (e.g. IAnalyticsRepository or AnalyticsPort or AnalyticsRepositoryPort) and specifies it belongs in the domain layer
Calls out the /analytics/live raw db query as a distinct, additional violation — separate from the route importing the concrete repository class

evals.prompt: The billing module shipped last sprint. Can you do an architecture review on it and let me know if there are structural issues we should address before the codebase grows?
evals.expected_output: The reviewer should identify the fat-controller anti-pattern, the absence of a service and repository layer, embedded business logic and Stripe calls in routes, direct DB queries, and missing DI. The deeper differentiators: (1) identifies the Stripe singleton at module scope as bypassing SecretsProvider (a project-specific convention) and lacking an injection seam. (2) Notes the partial-failure risk in /billing/cancel: Stripe cancel executes before the DB update with no compensation if the update fails. (3) Identifies that the webhook handler is one massive handler containing 3 distinct business events that each warrant a separate use case. (4) Recommends a StripeAdapter port/adapter pair, not just 'inject Stripe'.
expectations: Identifies the partial-failure / atomicity risk in /billing/cancel: stripe.subscriptions.cancel() is called before the DB update, so a DB failure after the Stripe call leaves state inconsistent with no rollback
Notes that the Stripe client is instantiated at module scope bypassing a secrets/config abstraction — it lacks an injection seam for testing and violates the adapter pattern

Identifies that the webhook handler embeds at least 3 distinct business event handlers (subscription updated, subscription deleted, invoice.payment_failed) inline rather than delegating to separate use cases or handlers
Recommends a StripeAdapter or StripePort (port/adapter pair) as the correct abstraction — not just 'inject the Stripe client'
Notes that GET /billing/invoices has a write side effect (upsert into DB) making it non-idempotent and violating HTTP GET semantics — and that this decision logic belongs in a use case, not a route
